question: What first drew you to youth work as a career?
lookingFor: Genuine motivation grounded in real experience, not a generic 'I like helping people' answer.

bullets: Name a specific moment or relationship that sparked the interest
Show understanding that youth work is different from just liking young people
Connect it to why you want to study it formally now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started volunteering as a youth club helper when I was sixteen, mostly running games nights, and what hooked me wasn't the fun parts but watching a shy younger boy come out of his shell over a few months just because someone consistently showed up for him. That made me realise good youth work isn't about entertaining people, it's about being a steady, trusted adult in someone's life. I want to study it properly now because I know there's a whole body of theory and practice behind what I was doing instinctively, and I want to do it well rather than just by feel.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I've always loved kids' with nothing more specific
Describing youth work as babysitting or entertainment
No mention of any real contact with young people
followUps: What have you learned since that first experience that surprised you?

question: Tell us about your experience working with young people so far.
lookingFor: Concrete, varied experience with reflection on what it taught them, not just a list of placements.

bullets: Name specific settings, such as a youth club, school, sports coaching, or faith group
Describe a specific role or responsibility, not just attendance
Reflect on one thing that experience taught about young people or yourself
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been a volunteer assistant at my local youth centre for just over a year, helping run a Friday drop-in for eleven to sixteen year olds, and before that I coached under-13s football for two seasons. The youth centre work taught me the most, because unlike coaching there's no set activity to hide behind, you just have to be present and build relationships with young people who don't have to be there. I learned quickly that consistency matters more than being the fun one, the same three or four young people started opening up to me once they realised I'd be there every week.

commonMistakes: Listing placements with no detail or reflection
Only mentioning structured settings like school with no informal contact
Overstating experience that was really just a single one-off event
followUps: What was the hardest moment in that experience and how did you handle it?

question: Why do you want to study youth work here specifically?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to course structure or placements, not generic praise.

bullets: Reference a specific course feature, such as the placement model or a professional qualification link
Connect it to a personal need or goal
Show awareness of what makes the course distinct
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course leads to the professional youth work qualification recognised by the sector body, and the fact that placements start in first year rather than final year matters a lot to me, because I learn best by testing theory against real practice straight away. I also read about the detached youth work module, which is an area I've only seen from the outside and want to actually learn properly, since a lot of the young people I want to work with in the future never walk into a youth club in the first place. It felt like a course built for people who want to practice, not just study the subject from a distance.

commonMistakes: Praise that could apply to any university
No mention of the professional qualification or placement structure
Confusing youth work with a related but different course like social work
followUps: What would you find hardest about the placement side of the course?

question: In your own words, what is youth work?
lookingFor: An understanding that youth work is a relationship-based, voluntary, educational process, not just activities.

bullets: State that it centres on the young person's own agenda and voluntary participation
Distinguish it from simply organising activities or entertainment
Mention the relationship and trust-building element
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Youth work is an informal, educational relationship with young people that starts from where they are and what matters to them, rather than a fixed curriculum. The activities, whether it's sport, art, or just hanging out in a youth club, are really a vehicle for building trust, because young people won't open up to an adult who hasn't earned that first. What makes it different from teaching or childcare is that young people choose to be there and can choose to leave, so the whole relationship has to be earned rather than assumed.

commonMistakes: Describing it purely as running fun activities
Confusing it with formal education or childminding
Giving a vague answer with no reference to voluntary participation
followUps: Why does it matter that participation is voluntary?

question: How is youth work different from teaching?
lookingFor: A clear grasp of the informal, non-compulsory, relationship-led nature of youth work versus the formal curriculum of teaching.

bullets: Contrast compulsory attendance and curriculum in teaching with voluntary, young-person-led youth work
Note the different power balance and setting
Show respect for teaching rather than dismissing it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A teacher works within a set curriculum that a young person has to attend and be assessed on, so however good the relationship is, there's always that formal structure underneath. Youth work has no compulsory attendance and no fixed syllabus, a young person can walk out of a session and never come back, which completely changes the power balance and means you have to build trust rather than rely on authority. I don't think one is more important than the other, they just reach young people in different ways, and some young people who've switched off from school will still respond to a youth worker precisely because it doesn't feel like school.

commonMistakes: Suggesting teaching is less valuable or less skilled
Missing the voluntary participation distinction entirely
Conflating youth work with being a teaching assistant
followUps: Can youth work happen inside a school?

question: What's the difference between a youth worker and a social worker?
lookingFor: Understanding of the distinct remits, statutory intervention versus voluntary and universal practice, while recognising overlap.

bullets: Note social work often involves statutory duties, assessments, and safeguarding case management
Note youth work is typically voluntary, universal, and focused on relationship and development rather than intervention
Acknowledge the two professions overlap and work together, especially around vulnerable young people
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A social worker usually has a statutory role, they're often involved because there's a legal duty to assess risk or intervene in a family, and the young person doesn't get to opt out of that relationship. A youth worker's relationship is voluntary and universal, open to any young person who wants to walk in, and it's built around development and trust rather than assessment or case management. In practice the two roles often meet, a youth worker might be the one who notices something's wrong and refers it on, so I see it less as a rivalry and more as different points of contact around the same young person.

commonMistakes: Saying the two jobs are basically the same
Dismissing social work as only about removing children from families
Not recognising where the roles overlap in practice
followUps: When would a youth worker need to involve a social worker?

question: Youth work is often described as voluntary. Why does that principle matter so much in practice?
lookingFor: Real understanding that voluntary participation shapes engagement, power, and trust, not just a textbook definition.

bullets: Explain that young people choose to attend and can leave, which changes the power dynamic
Link it to why trust has to be earned rather than assumed
Give a practical implication, such as not being able to force participation or disclosure
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Because a young person can walk away at any point, a youth worker never has automatic authority the way a teacher or parent might, you have to actually earn the right to be listened to. That changes how you work day to day, you can't force someone to join in an activity or talk about something they don't want to, so you end up relying on patience and consistency rather than instruction. I think it's actually what makes the trust real when it does happen, because the young person chose it rather than being told to.

commonMistakes: Treating it as just a definitional detail rather than something that shapes daily practice
Suggesting a youth worker can compel participation for the young person's own good
No concrete example of what it means in practice
followUps: What would you do if a young person who clearly needed support kept refusing to engage?

question: Has any book, article, or writer shaped how you think about youth work?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine wider reading beyond the syllabus, with the ability to explain the idea in their own words.

bullets: Name something specific, not just 'I read about youth work online'
Explain the core idea in their own words
Connect it to their own practice or thinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I came across a piece on detached youth work that described the worker's job as going to where young people already are rather than waiting for them to come to a building, and it genuinely changed how I thought about the field. Before that I assumed youth work meant a youth club with a building and a rota. It made me realise the young people who might need it most are often the ones least likely to walk through a youth centre door, and reaching them takes a completely different set of skills, patience, and just being visible and approachable without an agenda.

commonMistakes: Naming a source vaguely without explaining the idea
Picking something clearly unrelated to youth work to sound impressive
No personal reflection on how it changed their thinking
followUps: Did that reading change anything about how you approached your own volunteering?

question: What do you understand by safeguarding in a youth work setting?
lookingFor: A basic but accurate grasp of a youth worker's duty to protect young people from harm and to know when and how to act.

bullets: Define safeguarding as protecting young people's welfare and responding appropriately to concerns
Mention the duty to report concerns to a designated safeguarding lead rather than handling it alone
Show awareness that safeguarding is everyone's responsibility, not a side task
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Safeguarding is about protecting young people from harm, whether that's abuse, neglect, or exploitation, and making sure the environment and the adults around them are safe. What I understand is that if a young person tells me something worrying, or I notice a change in their behaviour that concerns me, my job isn't to investigate it myself or promise total secrecy, it's to stay calm, listen, and pass it on to a designated safeguarding lead as soon as possible. I know it can feel like a betrayal of trust in the moment, but I'd rather the young person be safe than keep a secret that puts them at risk.

commonMistakes: Promising to keep everything a young person says confidential no matter what
Describing safeguarding only as paperwork or box-ticking
Vague answer with no mention of the reporting procedure
followUps: What would you say to a young person before they disclose something, about the limits of confidentiality?

question: A fifteen-year-old you've built a strong relationship with tells you something is wrong at home but begs you not to tell anyone. What do you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning that balances trust with the duty to protect, landing on appropriate escalation rather than either extreme.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine tension between honouring trust and the duty of care
Explain they would be honest about the limits of confidentiality, ideally before or during the disclosure
Land on reporting to the designated safeguarding lead while trying to preserve the relationship
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want that young person to know I take what they've said seriously, and I'd be honest with them that I can't promise to keep something like this fully secret if it means they might not be safe, that's not me choosing rules over them, it's me making sure the right people can actually help. I'd try to explain what happens next in a way that doesn't feel like a betrayal, for example that I'll speak to our safeguarding lead and that I'll stay involved rather than disappearing once I've reported it. It would be a hard conversation, but staying silent to protect the relationship in the short term could leave them at risk, and I don't think that's actually kind.

commonMistakes: Promising absolute confidentiality to keep the young person's trust
Reporting without any thought for how it affects the relationship
Freezing and not committing to a course of action
followUps: How would you rebuild trust with them afterward if they felt betrayed?

question: What does it mean to 'empower' a young person, and how is that different from just helping them?
lookingFor: Understanding of youth work's core value of building capacity and agency rather than creating dependency.

bullets: Distinguish doing something for a young person from supporting them to do it themselves
Give a concrete example of empowering practice
Show awareness of the risk of creating dependency
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Helping someone can sometimes mean solving the problem for them, which feels good in the moment but doesn't leave them any more capable next time. Empowering is slower and less satisfying to watch, it means standing back and supporting a young person to make the phone call themselves, fill in the form themselves, or work out the argument with a friend themselves, even if I could do it faster. I saw this with a young person at my youth club who wanted to complain about being unfairly excluded from a school trip, my instinct was to sort it for her, but instead we practiced what she'd say and she went in and did it herself, and I think that mattered more than the outcome.

commonMistakes: Describing empowerment as just giving advice
No example distinguishing it from doing things for someone
Missing the risk of fostering dependency
followUps: Is there ever a time you should just step in and do it for them?

question: What is detached youth work, and what skills does it need that a youth club setting might not?
lookingFor: Accurate knowledge of detached practice plus insight into the extra skills of working without a building or fixed programme.

bullets: Define detached work as going out to where young people naturally gather rather than waiting in a building
Note it requires initiating contact with no captive audience or activity to fall back on
Mention safety and boundary skills specific to working in outdoor or unsupervised spaces
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Detached youth work means going out to parks, street corners, or wherever young people already spend time, instead of running a fixed session in a building and hoping they turn up. It needs a different kind of confidence, because there's no activity to hide behind and no captive audience, you have to be comfortable approaching a group of strangers and earning the right to talk to them with nothing but yourself. It also demands sharper judgement about safety and boundaries, since you're working in open, unsupervised spaces rather than a controlled room, so knowing when to step back matters just as much as knowing how to start a conversation.

commonMistakes: Confusing detached work with simply holding youth clubs outdoors
Not mentioning the initiating-contact challenge
Ignoring the extra safety and boundary considerations
followUps: How would you handle a group that seemed hostile to you approaching?

question: How would you make sure a youth club or group you're running feels welcoming to young people from different backgrounds?
lookingFor: Genuine grasp of anti-oppressive, inclusive practice, not a token statement about diversity.

bullets: Recognise that inclusion is active, not just an open-door policy
Mention checking your own assumptions and being led by young people's own identities and needs
Give a concrete practical example, such as varying activities or imagery to reflect the group
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think inclusion happens just because the door is technically open to everyone, you have to actively notice who isn't in the room and ask why. I'd start by checking my own assumptions, for example not assuming every young person celebrates the same holidays or has the same home situation, and by actually asking the young people what would make the space feel like theirs rather than deciding for them. At my current placement we changed the music and some of the activities after a few young people said the club felt geared toward one group, and attendance from a wider range of young people picked up noticeably afterward.

commonMistakes: A vague statement that 'everyone is welcome' with no active steps
Assuming inclusion is only about ethnicity and ignoring disability, gender, or class
Describing inclusion as something decided by staff without asking young people
followUps: How would you handle a young person in the group expressing a prejudiced view toward another member?

question: Give an example of a session or interaction that didn't go the way you expected, and what you learned from reflecting on it.
lookingFor: Honest reflective practice showing the ability to learn from experience, a core youth work skill.

bullets: Describe a real situation honestly, including what went wrong
Show genuine reflection, not just a description of events
Explain a specific change made to future practice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I once planned a whole session around a cooking activity because I thought it would get a quiet group talking, but almost nobody engaged and the session felt flat. Reflecting on it afterward, I realised I'd designed it around what I thought young people would enjoy rather than asking them, and cooking wasn't something that group cared about at all. The next week I asked them directly what they wanted to do, and even though the answer surprised me, just playing cards while we talked, the engagement was completely different. It taught me that my job is to follow their interests, not impose mine, however well-intentioned.

commonMistakes: Describing a session that went perfectly, avoiding real reflection
Blaming the young people for a session not working
No concrete change made afterward
followUps: How do you build reflection into your practice regularly, not just after something goes wrong?

question: How do you think social media is affecting the young people you'd be working with?
lookingFor: A balanced, current-awareness view that avoids moral panic while recognising real risks and benefits.

bullets: Avoid a purely negative or purely dismissive take, show balance
Mention specific effects, such as comparison, sleep, or access to support communities
Connect it to a practical implication for youth work practice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it cuts both ways. I've seen young people at my youth club find real support and community online, especially ones who feel isolated locally, but I've also seen the comparison culture hit their confidence hard, and constant notifications eating into sleep and face-to-face time. What worries me more than the platforms themselves is how little unstructured, offline time some young people get, which is actually part of why I think youth work matters, it's one of the few spaces left that's deliberately unplugged and about being present with other people.

commonMistakes: A purely alarmist take with no nuance
Dismissing the concern entirely as adults overreacting
No connection to what it means for youth work practice
followUps: Would you ever use social media as a tool in your youth work practice?

question: What do you understand about county lines or child criminal exploitation, and how might it show up in a youth work setting?
lookingFor: Current awareness of a serious safeguarding issue and understanding of the youth worker's role in noticing and responding, not investigating.

bullets: Define exploitation in basic accurate terms, young people groomed and coerced into carrying drugs or money for criminal networks
Mention warning signs a youth worker might notice, such as unexplained money, new relationships, or unexplained absences
Emphasise the youth worker's role is to notice and refer, not to investigate or confront alone
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: County lines is where criminal networks groom and exploit young people, often ones who are vulnerable or excluded, to carry or sell drugs across areas, frequently using coercion or debt rather than obvious force, which is why victims often don't see themselves as victims. In a youth work setting it might show up subtly, a young person suddenly having new items or money they can't explain, new older friends nobody's met, or unexplained absences and secretive behaviour. My role wouldn't be to play detective, it would be to notice the pattern, keep the relationship going so they still trust me, and raise it with a safeguarding lead rather than confronting them or the situation myself.

commonMistakes: No real understanding of what county lines actually means
Suggesting the youth worker should investigate or intervene directly
Framing exploited young people as criminals rather than victims
followUps: Why might an exploited young person resist help even when it's offered?

question: How would you handle a young person who's being disruptive and undermining a session for everyone else?
lookingFor: A calm, boundaried approach that addresses behaviour without shaming the young person or abandoning the group.

bullets: Show awareness of de-escalation over confrontation
Balance the needs of the individual with the needs of the group
Recognise disruptive behaviour often signals something underneath it worth understanding
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to call them out in front of everyone, that usually escalates things and makes them perform for an audience. I'd try to calmly redirect the group's attention and find a quiet moment to speak to that young person one on one, asking what's going on rather than just telling them to stop, because disruptive behaviour is often about something else, being tired, anxious, or wanting attention they're not getting elsewhere. I'd still be clear about the boundary that the behaviour can't continue because it affects everyone else, but I'd want them to know the boundary isn't personal and the door stays open.

commonMistakes: Publicly shaming or punishing the young person in front of the group
Ignoring the impact on the rest of the group
No boundary at all, letting disruption continue unchecked
followUps: What would you do if the behaviour kept happening despite that conversation?

question: How would you try to build a relationship with a young person who's clearly avoiding you and doesn't want to engage?
lookingFor: Patience and respect for the young person's pace, with understanding that trust can't be forced given voluntary participation.

bullets: Reject the idea of forcing engagement, respect their right to opt out
Describe low-pressure, consistent ways of staying present and approachable
Show patience, accepting it may take a long time or may not fully work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't chase them, because forcing it usually confirms whatever made them wary in the first place. I'd focus on just being consistently, calmly present, saying hello without expecting a response, being visibly around the same activities they might drift near, and letting them see over time that I'm not going anywhere and I'm not going to push. With one young person at my placement it took about two months of exactly that before he started sitting near the pool table I was running, and even then it was small talk for weeks before anything real came up. I've learned that patience isn't passive, it's actually the work.

commonMistakes: Pushing repeatedly for engagement, seeing avoidance as a problem to solve quickly
Giving up entirely rather than staying consistently present
Taking it personally rather than understanding it may not be about them
followUps: How do you keep your own morale up during that long, uncertain process?

question: Why might a youth worker need to work closely with schools or social services, and what challenges can that bring?
lookingFor: Understanding of multi-agency working and awareness of the tensions, such as differing priorities or confidentiality expectations.

bullets: Explain why joined-up working benefits the young person, sharing a fuller picture
Note the different priorities or cultures of each service
Mention the challenge of maintaining the young person's trust while sharing information appropriately
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A young person doesn't live their life in one setting, so a school, a social worker, and a youth worker often each see a different slice of the same picture, and putting those pieces together usually helps the young person more than any one service acting alone. The challenge is that each service has different priorities and different rules around what can be shared, a school might be focused on attendance and behaviour records while I'm focused on the relationship, and I have to be careful that working closely with other agencies doesn't make the young person feel like I'm just another authority reporting on them. Keeping that trust while still being a responsible partner is probably the hardest balance in the job.

commonMistakes: Describing partnership working as simply following instructions from other agencies
No mention of the trust or confidentiality tension involved
Suggesting youth work should stay entirely separate from other services
followUps: How would you explain to a young person why you're sharing information about them with a school?

subtopic: Statutory versus voluntary sector youth work
question: What's the difference between statutory and voluntary sector youth work, and does it matter to you which you end up in?
lookingFor: Basic sector knowledge and honest reflection on personal preference, showing awareness of trade-offs rather than indifference.

bullets: Define statutory, local authority funded and often targeted, versus voluntary or community sector, often universal and locally rooted
Note trade-offs such as funding stability versus flexibility and local trust
Give an honest personal view rather than a neutral non-answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Statutory youth work is usually run or commissioned by the local authority and often ends up targeted at young people already flagged as at risk, because that's where funding gets prioritised, while voluntary and community sector organisations tend to be more universal, open to anyone, and often have deeper roots and trust in a specific local area even if their funding is less stable. I'd honestly like to start in the voluntary sector, because I think the open-door, universal model is closer to why I got into this in the first place, though I know the funding insecurity that comes with it is a real downside I'd have to accept.

commonMistakes: Saying it doesn't matter without any real reasoning
Confusing statutory funding with a statutory duty to intervene
No awareness of the funding or trust trade-offs between sectors
followUps: What would you do if funding cuts threatened a service you were running?

question: How would you actually give young people a genuine say in how a youth service is run, rather than just asking their opinion?
lookingFor: Understanding that meaningful participation goes beyond consultation to shared decision-making, ideally with awareness of participation models like Hart's Ladder.

bullets: Distinguish tokenistic consultation from genuine shared decision-making
Reference a concrete mechanism, such as a youth forum, budget input, or co-designed programming
Show awareness that participation is a spectrum and even 'genuine' efforts can slip into tokenism
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There's a real difference between asking young people what they think and then doing whatever you were going to do anyway, and actually giving them power over a decision. I know Hart's Ladder of Participation frames a lot of what gets called consultation as barely above tokenism, because the adults still hold all the real control. I'd want to try things like a young people's forum with an actual budget they allocate themselves, or co-designing a term's programme with them from a blank page rather than a pre-made menu of options, because the moment they can see their decision genuinely changed something, that's when it stops being a box-ticking exercise.

commonMistakes: Describing a suggestion box or feedback form as genuine participation
No awareness of the difference between consultation and shared decision-making
Overpromising total youth control with no acknowledgment of practical limits like safety or budget
followUps: What would you do if young people voted for something the funding or policy couldn't actually support?

question: Youth work can be emotionally demanding, especially when you can't fix everything. How would you look after your own wellbeing?
lookingFor: Realistic self-awareness about the emotional cost of the work and concrete, sustainable strategies, not just 'I'll be fine.'

bullets: Acknowledge honestly that the work can be emotionally heavy and burnout is real
Describe specific, concrete coping strategies, such as supervision or debriefing
Show understanding that looking after yourself is part of being reliable for young people, not selfish
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think I'll be able to switch it off completely, and I don't think I should pretend I would, some situations will stay with me. What I've already started doing during my volunteering is talking things through with my supervisor after a hard session rather than carrying it home unprocessed, and being honest with myself about which parts are actually mine to solve and which aren't. I also try to keep something completely separate from youth work in my own life, for me that's running, because I think if the whole of my identity is wrapped up in this job, I'll burn out faster and actually be less useful to the young people who need me consistent.

commonMistakes: Claiming the emotional side won't affect them at all
No concrete strategy beyond vague statements like 'I'll manage'
Framing self-care as unimportant compared to the young people's needs
followUps: Has anything already tested your resilience in your experience so far?

question: A young person you work with adds you on social media and wants to be your friend outside sessions. How would you handle it?
lookingFor: Clear understanding of professional boundaries that protects both the young person and the worker, delivered without coldness.

bullets: Explain the boundary clearly and kindly rather than ignoring the request
Show understanding of why the boundary exists for safeguarding and role clarity
Avoid making the young person feel rejected personally
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't accept the request, but I also wouldn't want them to feel rejected, so I'd explain it directly rather than just silently ignoring it. I'd tell them it's not personal, it's a boundary I keep with everyone I work with, because staying just their youth worker rather than also being a friend on social media is actually what lets me keep being useful to them, professionally and safely, for as long as they need me. I'd rather have that slightly awkward conversation once than blur a line that protects both of us.

commonMistakes: Accepting the request to avoid an awkward conversation
Being so blunt about the boundary that it feels like a personal rejection
No mention of the safeguarding reasoning behind the boundary
followUps: What would you do if they seemed hurt or confused by your answer?

subtopic: A moment you influenced a young person
question: Tell us about a specific moment when you felt you made a real difference to a young person, however small.
lookingFor: A genuine, specific story that shows the applicant's understanding of what meaningful impact in youth work actually looks like.

bullets: Pick one specific, small moment rather than a vague general claim of impact
Explain what you actually did, not just the outcome
Reflect on why it mattered, tying it back to youth work values
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There was a girl at my youth club who never spoke in group activities and always sat at the edge, and one evening I just sat next to her at the edge too instead of trying to pull her into the group, and asked what she was drawing. We talked about nothing important for twenty minutes, but the next week she came and sat a little closer to the group on her own. It wasn't dramatic, nobody would have noticed from across the room, but it taught me that the real work often happens in those small, unforced moments rather than in anything I planned or ran.

commonMistakes: A vague, unverifiable claim of 'changing someone's life'
Focusing on the outcome with no description of what was actually done
Taking full credit as if the young person played no role themselves
followUps: How do you know it actually mattered to her, rather than assuming it did?

question: Where do you see yourself working after you graduate, and how does this course prepare you for it?
lookingFor: A grounded, specific direction connected honestly to the course, not an overly rigid or vague plan.

bullets: Give a realistic direction, ideally naming a setting or type of young people they want to work with
Connect it honestly to specific parts of the course, such as placements or specialist modules
Show openness to the path evolving
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd like to end up doing detached or outreach work with young people who've disengaged from school and other services, because that's the group I think gets left behind most easily. This course's early and varied placements matter a lot for that, since I'll get exposure to different settings before I have to specialise, and the module on working with vulnerable young people is exactly the grounding I'll need. I know the exact job title might look different by the time I graduate, but the direction, working with the young people who are hardest to reach, is one I'm sure about.

commonMistakes: An overly specific job title with no flexibility
No real connection between the goal and what the course actually offers
A goal that suggests youth work is a stepping stone to something else entirely
followUps: What's the first step you'd take after graduating to get there?
